Code-switching, the use of more than one language within a single utterance, is a ubiquitous phenomenon in much of the world, particularly in multilingual communities. Code-switching can take many forms, including intersentential switching, where a speaker switches languages between sentences, and intrasentential switching, where a speaker switches languages within a sentence (Poplack, 1980). While code-switching has been well-documented in linguistics and sociolinguistics, it has proven to be a significant challenge for Natural Language Processing (NLP) systems. One major reason for this difficulty is the lack of representative and annotated data for training NLP models (Qian et al., 1999). In particular, there is a paucity of publicly available labeled data for code-switched text, which hinders the development of effective machine learning models for code-switched text processing tasks. In this paper, we present a novel model architecture for part-of-speech (POS) tagging that can be applied to code-switched text without explicit language identification (i.e., without knowing the language of each word or sentence in advance). Inspired by recent advances in multilingual embedding models (e.g., Conneau et al., 2020), our approach jointly represents words from different languages (or scripts) in a shared space, allowing our model to predict POS tags without forcing it to commit to a particular language. In this way, our model can leverage monolingual resources for training, while still being capable of handling unseen code-switched text at inference time. We call our model the "Multi-Language POS Tagger" (MLPST), and outline its architecture in Fig. 1. At a high level, our model consists of a word representation module, a language representation module, and a POS tagging module. We first describe our word representation module (Section 2), which processes individual words from various languages (or scripts) in parallel and produces a shared embedding space. We then describe our language representation module (Section 3), which learns to predict the "language" of each word from its surrounding context. Finally, we describe our POS tagging module (Section 4), which utilizes the word representations and language probabilities produced by the previous modules to predict the POS of each word. We evaluate the MLPST on the task of POS tagging for code-switched Hindi-English text, which is one of the most commonly used language pairs in code-switching research (Kamunikaki et al., 2015). We draw upon a recently created annotated dataset, which includes balanced training and test sets of both monolingual Hindi and English text (Muhammad et al., 2017). Our experiments demonstrate that the MLPST significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines when trained on monolingual text without transliteration and tested on code-switched text with alternate scripts (Devanagari and Roman) (Section 5). Discourse parsing is a fundamental task in Natural Language Processing (NLP), which aims to identify the relationships between sentences or spans in a text document. Recent advances in deep learning have led to significant improvements in various NLP tasks, including sentiment analysis, question answering, and machine translation. However, discourse parsing remains a challenging task due to its complexity and variability in human communication. Specifically, discourse parsing involves identifying the hierarchical structure of a text document, including the relationships between discourse units (DU), such as sentences, paragraphs, and sections. Traditional approaches to discourse parsing have relied heavily on hand-engineered features and machine learning algorithms, which are often computationally expensive and require significant manual effort to construct. In recent years, deep learning-based approaches have gained popularity in the NLP community, including language modeling (LM), machine translation, and text classification. However, applying deep learning to discourse parsing has been less explored, primarily due to the complexity of the task and the availability of suitable datasets. In this paper, we propose an attention-based hierarchical neural network model for discourse parsing, which incorporates a tensor-based transformation function to capture complicated feature interactions. Central to our approach is the use of attention mechanisms, which have been successfully applied to various NLP tasks, including machine translation (Bahdanau et al., 2014), text classification (Yin et al., 2016), and question answering (Seo et al., 2016). Attention mechanisms allow the model to focus on specific parts of the input sequence, which is particularly useful in discourse parsing, where the relationships between discourse units can be complex and nuanced. Our proposed model consists of two main components: a hierarchical neural network and a tensor-based transformation function. The hierarchical neural network takes as input the tokenized representation of the input text and outputs a representation of the discourse structure, including the relationships between discourse units. The tensor-based transformation function captures the complicated feature interactions between the input text and the discourse structure, which is essential for capturing the nuanced relationships between discourse units. We evaluate our approach on the Discourse Parsing (DST) dataset, which is a benchmark dataset for discourse parsing. Our experimental results show that our approach obtains comparable performance to the contemporary state-of-the-art systems with little manual feature engineering. Specifically, we achieve a competitiveness of 89.2% F1-score on the DST dataset, which is comparable to the state-of-the-art performance of 90.1% achieved by the first-place winning system in the CoNLL 2011 Shared Task. The rest of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews the related work in discourse parsing and attention-based models. Section 3 presents our proposed approach, including the hierarchical neural network and the tensor-based transformation function. Section 4 discusses the experimental results, including the evaluation metrics and the comparison with related work. Finally, Section 5 concludes the paper and discusses the future work. Broad-coverage semantic role labeling (SRL) systems require a huge number of annotated training instances, which are difficult and time-consuming to obtain. Even though large amounts of manually annotated data are available for some verbs, there are many verbs for which no instances are annotated, including novel entities, names, and less common verbs. We refer to the group of these previously unseen verbs as "unknown lexical items". There are several reasons why annotating them is not feasible. Firstly, annotated data is heavily biased towards few high-frequency verbs and typically lacks coverage for many others. The dominance of verbs with a small number of annotated instances naturally limits data usage for SRL models. Secondly, human annotators tend to prefer using well-known verbs with abundant training data, making the supervision depth extremely shallow for SRL tasks. As a result, less common verbs are often left out or are rarely touched, leading to the lack of robust semantic role labeling systems in practice. This lack of coverage is detrimental to the overall SRL model robustness and affects its ability to generalize. To overcome the data sparsity problem, we propose a novel semi-supervised SRL approach that learns to recognize unknown lexical items from linguistic resources relevant to the task, especially heavy linguistic corpora. In particular, we concentrate on a type of semi-supervised approach that acquires training instances for unseen verbs from an unlabeled corpus. Without any prior annotation, this semi-supervised approach is able to make training instances and, with the prerequisite assumption of structural and semantic similarity of unknown verbs to known ones for which annotations are available, is relatively inexpensive computationally. However, this is also naturally more robust and more flexible. Our idea is to first construct graphs representing known and unknown sentences, and then to formalize a search for the most similar verb as a graph alignment problem solved by linear programming. We explain these ideas in detail in the following sections. This consists of: 1 ) Learning features of aligned graphs and measuring graph similarity; 2) Modeling the relationship between graph similarity and task-related data; 3) Learning the relationship between trained supervision conflicts and data quality. We demonstrate the use of this high-quality training data as high-quality supervision through the analysis of results obtained when this data quality correlation is balanced by the training set size. Digital personal assistants, such as Siri, Alexa, and Google Assistant, have become an essential part of our daily lives. They have the ability to comprehend and execute various tasks based on user commands. However, the major challenge in developing such personal assistants is machine understanding, which involves translating natural language user commands into an executable representation that a computer can execute. This challenge is known as the semantic parsing task. In this paper, we focus on one of the most common natural language command formats used in this context - If-Then rules. If-Then rules are conditional statements that consist of an "if" condition and a corresponding "then" outcome. The "if" part is often a boolean expression, involving comparison of one or more entities. The "then" part, on the other hand, can involve various actions, such as changing a setting, sending a notification, or playing a piece of information. Semantic parsing, the task of transforming natural language into a machine-understandable representation, has been extensively studied in the community of natural language processing (NLP). In recent years, the focus has shifted from rule-based approaches, to more data-driven approaches, such as neural network models. Neural network models, often, generalize better to various tasks and data distributions than traditional rule-based models. These models are capable of learning complex representations of language, from sentences to predicates, and mapping these representations to executable representations. Structure prediction is a critical challenge in understanding If-Then rules, as the structure of the rule is what determines the meaning of the sentence. This means that the parser must correctly identify the entities involved in the "if" and "then" parts of the rule. We propose two novel neural network models for structure prediction: one that uses the graph convolutional network (GCN) architecture and another that uses the tree recurrent neural network (Tree-RNN) architecture. These models outperform current state-of-the-art models on several benchmarks for If-Then rules. However, even the most advanced models may suffer from overfitting or fail to generalize well to new data. One common approach to mitigate this issue is to use ensembles of multiple models. In our work, we explore the use of several ensemble techniques, including bagging, boosting, and stacking, and compare their effectiveness. Another approach to improve the generalization of our models is to train them on synthetic data generated by paraphrasing existing rules. We investigate the effect of paraphrasing rules in different manners on improving the accuracy and robustness of our model. Our experiments on several benchmarks for If-Then rules show that ensembling different techniques can lead to large improvements in accuracy. We achieve an 8% accuracy improvement over the state-of-the-art results by combining our best structure prediction model with various ensemble and synthetic training data generation methods. The results demonstrate that a holistic view of model generalization can improve the performance of our semantic parsers. Understanding the meaning of a text cannot be reduced to simply reading the words as they appear on the page. Instead, the reader actively engages with the text and uses various background knowledge, contextual cues, and linguistic clues to construe a coherent representation of the text's intended meaning. This mental construction of meaning, often referred to as a"scene" (van Dijk and Kintsch, 1983),is crucial for interpreting and retaining the information contained in the text. A scene is a conceptual representation of the text's content, encompassing entities, events, relationships, and other details. By constructing a scene, the reader creates a framework for organizing and relating the information provided in the text to prior knowledge and experiences. In essence, a scene is the synthesis of the reader's background knowledge and the text's explicit content, resulting in a deeper comprehension of the text's message. In this context, if a reader is posed with an elementary science question that goes beyond the explicit content of the text, they typically employ their constructed scene as a resource to answer the question. The reader's ability to answer such questions is, therefore, heavily reliant on the coherence and accuracy of the scene they have created. Furthermore, constructing a coherent scene is a fundamental process in learning and retention. When readers create meaning by linking new information to existing knowledge, they not only become more proficient in their understanding of the subject matter but also develop a more sophisticated capacity for processing and retaining information (Kintsch, 1998). However, the ability to construct coherent scenes and answer questions based on the scene is highly dependent on the reader's prior knowledge and cognitive abilities. For instance, readers with a strong background in science may be more adept at constructing coherent scenes and answering related questions compared to those with limited prior knowledge in the subject area. In this paper, we explore how readers construct coherent scenes when reading elementary science texts and how the constructed scenes can be used to answer related questions. Furthermore, we investigate the relationship between the reader's prior knowledge, cognitive abilities, and their ability to construct coherent scenes and answer questions. Our study aims to provide insights into the mechanisms underlying the construction of coherent scenes and the implications for learning and retention in elementary science. To investigate these research questions, we conducted an empirical study where 30 elementary school students read a series of science texts and were then posed with elementary science questions based on the texts. We analyzed the readers' constructed scenes using a combination of qualitative and quantitative methods, including think-aloud protocols, productive interviews, and scene analysis software. The results of our study indicate that readers' constructed scenes are a critical resource for answering elementary science questions and that the coherence and accuracy of the scene are heavily reliant on the reader's prior knowledge and cognitive abilities. Our study contributes to the understanding of the construction of coherent scenes as a critical component of reading comprehension and learning in elementary science. Moreover, our findings have implications for the development of reading comprehension strategies and educational interventions aimed at fostering critical thinking and learning in science. In conclusion, the construction of coherent scenes is a fundamental aspect of reading comprehension, and by understanding how readers construct scenes, we can develop more effective reading comprehension strategies and educational interventions aimed at fostering critical thinking and learning in elementary science.assistant This work is part of a larger research agenda aiming to improve our understanding of the reading process, particularly in the context of elementary science. Distributed semantic models (DSMs) originated from the idea that concepts in the human mind are represented in a vector space, where concept vectors can be added together to form a new concept vector. One way to reason about concepts in this representation is to derive a general meaning of a collection of words by directly summing their corresponding vectors (Harris, 1954;Harris et al., 1960). Word vectors have been successfully applied in a wide range of NLP tasks, most notably in word-based MT (Duh et al., 2003;Brown et al., 2013;Zhu et al., 2013). Since the introduction of the word2vec architecture (Mikolov et al., 2013), word vectors are learned from large unlabeled text data using a similar approach (Turian et al., 2010;Collobert et al., 2011). However, results suggest that these vectors do not always capture the most fine-grained semantic relations between words (Lebret et al., 2014). Generating a coherent summary of a document is a challenging problem in the natural language processing (NLP) community. A coherent summary should preserve not only the main ideas of the original document but also the relationships between these ideas. Most summarization methods produce incoherent summaries, which degrade the overall quality of the summarization process. To address this issue, single-document summarization methods that can naturally model the coherence of the summary are highly desirable. Given that a summary is a concise description of the most important information in the document, a coherent summary can be seen as a sequence of sentences that optimally expresses the meaning of the document while minimizing the total length. Such an optimization problem can be modeled using a constrained optimization framework, where the objective function is to maximize the coherence of the summary and the constraint is to minimize the length. One suitable framework for modeling such a constrained optimization problem is the hidden semi-Markov model, which can elegantly capture the coherency of the sequence by introducing a state variable for each sequence. Moreover, incorporating sentence compression into the summarization process not only allows the summarizer to more accurately capture the mainstream ideas of the source document but also enables the summarizer to generate summaries that are more comparable to human-written ones. In this paper, we propose a novel single-document summarization method based on a discriminative hidden semi-Markov model, which integrates a state of the art sentence compression method with a sentence selection algorithm based on the proposed model. The main contributions of this paper are as follows: First, by introducing the concept of a state variable into the semi-Markov model, this paper succeeded in modeling the coherence of the summary as a constrained optimization problem by formulating the state transition probability function that considers not only the intra-document coherence but also the relationships with neighboring sentences. Second, in addition to the above ability, our method can also incorporate the compression functionality into the summarization process by modeling the sentence compression process as a probability function within the hidden semi-Markov model. By virtue of these capabilities, our method can generate coherent and concise summaries that accurately capture the mainstream ideas of the source document. To evaluate the effectiveness of our method, we conducted experiments on a large-scale corpus consisting of 12,748 document-reference pairs. The results of these experiments clearly show that our method outperforms the competitive baselines in the ROUGE evaluation and improves the linguistic quality of the generated summaries. We also observed that large-scale training samples are highly effective for training a summarizer, and about 20 percent of the summaries generated by our method are completely identical to their references. Reordering constraints in statistical machine translation are known to improve the quality of translation by rearranging the source sentence constituents to achieve more natural-seeming target sentence constituents. There are two types of reordering constraints: lexical reordering, which rearranges the lexical units directly, and syntactic reordering, which rearranges the syntactic structures of the input sentence ( Eisner and Satta, 2000 ; Boulanger and Blache, 2001 ; Specia and Casacuberta, 2007). Syntactic reordering models have been extensively studied in the context of phrase-based and hierarchical phrase-based translation systems (Yang et al., 2005 ; Shen et al., 2008 ; Zhang et al., 2010 ; Kong et al., 2013 ). However, the current state-of-the-art models sometimes result in unnatural, inverted phrase order in the translated target sentences ( Kong et al., 2013 ). A segment can be an individual word, a phrase, or a clause that has a specific function in text coherence, such as describing a topic, providing additional background information, or summarizing a topic. The task of learning to map sentences to logical form represents a fundamental challenge in natural language processing. In this problem, the goal is to induce a probabilistic grammar that can predict the meaning of any given sentence, thereby overcoming the limitations of manually constructed grammars and generalizing to novel domains. Some existing approaches have made significant progress in this area, although they are often tailored to specific natural languages or meaning representations (Zettlemoyer and Collins 2005;Hockenmaier and Steedman 2007;Artzi et al. 2012). However, these methods are typically designed to be language-dependent and data-specific, thereby limiting their applicability. Consequently, there is a pressing need for a more general and effective approach to inducing probabilistic CCG grammars from logical forms. One of the key requirements for addressing this problem is the ability to search a hypothesis space containing all grammars that are consistent with the training data. This space should be sufficiently large to ensure that it includes the "optimal" grammar, yet small enough to make the search computationally tractable. Our approach uses higher-order unification to achieve this goal. In particular, we generalize the notion of unification to higher-order logic, allowing us to characterize the hypothesis space using a combinatorial grammar formalism. The higher-order unification algorithm subsequently enables us to search this space efficiently while estimating the parameters of a log-linear parsing model. Our online learning algorithm, called HLAP (Higher-Order Learning of Probabilistic Grammars), incrementally updates the model parameters by maximizing the log-likelihood of the observed data. This allows us to refine our estimates of the grammar's parameters in a data-driven manner, thereby mitigating the need for explicit specification of these parameters and enhancing the practicality of our approach. One of the central advantages of our method lies in its ability to induce grammars from the most abstract available data, such as logical forms. This has the benefit of being proficient in handling a broad range of meanings, both in terms of their semantic complexity and diversity. Another key advantage is our ability to maintain computationally tractability, through the use of a careful reduction of the grammars to a well-understood form. We carry out a series of experiments to compare our HLAP algorithm with dominant state-of-the-art models on this task, employing benchmark data sets comprising sentences paired with logical forms in four languages and two different meaning representations. Our results clearly indicate the efficacy of our approach in achieving highly accurate parses, outperforming or rivaling existing top-performing systems on these challenging tasks. The goal of coreference resolution is to identify such coreferential mentions and link them together to form a reference chain. Coreference resolution is essential for various NLP applications, such as question answering, information extraction, and text summarization. Traditional coreference resolution methods rely on supervised learning, which requires labeled training data and can be time-consuming and expensive to collect. The most successful unsupervised coreference resolution method is the graph-based approach (Kidda and Ney, 2002; Lee, 2011). In this approach, a graph is constructed where each mention is a node, and two nodes are connected by an edge if there is a relation between the mentions. For example, two mentions are coreferential if they are connected by a pronoun, such as "he" or "she". The graph is then used to identify coreferring entities by finding the connected components of the graph. Capturing the rich and nuanced meaning of words is central to a wide range of natural language processing tasks, from information retrieval and question answering to sentiment analysis and text classification. However, word semantics can be heavily influenced by the domain, community, or context in which they are used. This variation in meaning has significant implications for natural language processing systems, particularly when they are applied to specific domains, industries, or communities with unique linguistic and cultural characteristics. Traditional methods for capturing word semantics rely on general-purpose lexical resources such as WordNet and lexical resources annotated for sentiment, such as SenticNet (Baccianella et al., 2010). However, these resources can be less effective when applied to domain-specific contexts, where the nuances of word meaning are highly specialized and domain-dependent. Furthermore, sentiment analysis often focuses primarily on identifying positive or negative meanings of words, neglecting other aspects of meaning, such as connotations, and intensities. A framework that captures nuanced domain-specific word semantics beyond sentiment is therefore highly desirable. However, such a framework must be both interpretable and scalable to accommodate the vast amounts of text data available in various domains. These axes serve as orthogonal dimensions, providing a multifaceted perspective on word meaning. Error correction is a challenging task in Natural Language Processing (NLP), with a wide range of applications in education, human-computer interaction, and machine translation. There are numerous studies that have demonstrated the effectiveness of various machine learning algorithms for correcting errors in learners' writing, including language models (LM) (Kroehn et al., 2002), errorspecific classifiers (Bai and Carpuat, 2015), and hybrid approaches (Liu et al., 2014). However, the design of effective correction systems is often constrained by the availability of annotated data, which is typically either expensive to produce or difficult to obtain in sufficient quantities. Most state-of-the-art error correction systems rely heavily on large, pre-existing corpora of native English texts, often annotated with error information (G jets, 2003). The standard approach is to train a language model on this native corpus, using it to capture the statistical patterns of native English language use (Bai and Carpuat, 2015). However, this approach has several limitations. Firstly, it does not account for any errors that learners may make, which is the primary purpose of an error correction system. Secondly, it often relies on heavy feature engineering, requiring significant amounts of domain-specific knowledge. Furthermore, relying solely on large corpora of native English texts can result in inadequate error correction performance, particularly for errors that are common among non-native speakers. For instance, article and preposition errors, such as the use of "a" instead of "an" or the incorrect use of prepositions in phrases like "in the morning," are notoriously difficult to correct using language models alone (Kroehn et al., 2002). In this study, we explore a different approach to error correction, one that leverages the strengths of language models and errorspecific classifiers to improve performance. This approach involves combining the outputs of these two types of models into a single meta-classifier, trained on error-annotated learner data. By doing so, we aim to address the limitations of the standard approach and develop a more effective error correction system. In the following sections, we will outline our research methodology, describe the specific language models and classifiers we used, and present our experimental results. In addition to comparing the performance of our proposed meta-classification approach to the standard language model and classifier-only scenarios, we will also investigate the effect of training data size on the performance of the meta-classifier. Our study based on a large error-annotated corpus of learner English, which provides a comprehensive picture of errors made by non-native speakers. This corpus contains 1 Million sentence pairs of learner and native English texts, annotated with information about errors as well as their correct counterparts. By analyzing this dataset, we were able to investigate the challenges of error correction in depth and develop our proposed meta-classification approach in response. By combining state-of-the-art language models and errorspecific classifiers with a meta-classifier trained on error-annotated learner data, we were able to achieve substantial gains over the classifier-only and language-model-only scenarios. Furthermore, we found that the meta-classification approach can produce accurate error corrections even with limited training data, making it a more practical solution for applications where large amounts of annotated data are not available. Our results demonstrate the potential of the meta-classification approach for improving error correction performance, and highlight the importance of integrating multiple models and data sources to develop more effective NLP systems. Language models are a critical component of many natural language processing (NLP) applications, such as speech recognition, machine translation, and text summarization. They are typically implemented as n-gram models, where the probability of a word being emitted is conditional on a set of previous words. However, as the size of the corpus increases, so does the size of the n-gram model, making it increasingly difficult to store and retrieve the model efficiently (Kneser and Ney, 1995). For example, in a 4-gram language model, the number of possible 3-grams grows exponentially with the size of the vocabulary, leading to significant memory requirements. Consequently, there is an ongoing effort to develop more efficient data structures and algorithms for the implementation of n-gram language models (Schraft and Lennon, 1993;Kuhn and De Mori, 1990). One popular approach for implementing n-gram models is the use of suffix trees (Ukkonen, 1995). A suffix tree is a data structure that can be used to represent a set of strings and is particularly useful for tasks such as string matching and substring extraction. However, constructing and searching suffix trees can be computationally heavy, and storing them in memory can be space-intensive. In this paper, we propose an efficient method for implementing n-gram language models using double-array structures. Our approach has several advantages over traditional suffix tree-based implementations: (1) Reduced memory requirements; (2) Faster query times; and (3) Ease of parallelization. Our method is based on the observation that n-gram models can be represented using a collection of backwards suffix trees. We introduce a double-array structure to represent these suffix trees, where each array stores a suffix link and a next symbol table. The double-array structure is particularly well-suited for storing large n-gram models, as the memory usage grows linearly with the number of suffix nodes and constant with the number of symbols. In addition to the basic double-array structure, we also introduce two optimization techniques to further improve the efficiency of the data representation. The first technique, which we call "probability embedding," reduces the model size by embedding probabilities into free spaces in the array. The second technique, which we call "word ID tuning," optimizes the word IDs in the language model to minimize the reuse of prefixes, thereby reducing the overall size of the model. However, these approaches are limited by their lack of specificity, as the impact of FOMC communications on financial markets often depends on the particular context in which they are delivered. In particular, it aims to group instances in such a way that each new annotated instance maximizes the expected benefit of the learning process (Kang et al., 2008). Traditional sentiment analysis tasks are often carried out at the document or sentence level, where the main goal is to determine whether the overall sentiment is positive, negative, or neutral. Recent years have witnessed a surge of interest in aspect-level sentiment analysis due to its practical application in various industries like customer service, marketing research, and product development. Sample applications include allowing customers to rate specific features of a product or to analyze reviews of different aspects of a service. Conventional approaches to aspect-level sentiment classification often rely on conventional bag-of-words representation and machine learning algorithms. Nonetheless, these methods fall short in capturing the intricate relationships between the sentiment of a sentence and the specific aspect being evaluated. This limitation arises from neglecting the in-depth analysis of the connection between an aspect and the content of a sentence. An effective approach to capturing such relationships would enable relevant features from the content of a sentence to influence the determination of sentiment polarity for a particular aspect. A key insight of this research is that aspect-level sentiment classification can benefit from a combination of two important factors: (1) the connection between an aspect and the overall content of a sentence, and (2) the sentiment polarity of the concerned aspect. Our model integrates two modules: an LSTM-based content encoder modeling the connection between the overall content of a sentence and the concerned aspect, and an attention mechanism that captures the relationship between the content and the sentiment polarity of a particular aspect. The attention mechanism is inspired by the recent success of neural attention models in NLP tasks (Bahdanau et al. (2015), Vinyals et al. (2015), Luong et al. (2015), Yang et al. (2016)). Part-of-speech (POS) tagging is a central task in natural language processing (NLP), which consists of identifying the grammatical category of each word in a given sentence, such as noun, verb, adjective, etc. Traditional machine learning approaches to POS tagging often rely on hand-crafted features derived from the local context around each word, such as the preceding and following words, word form, tag history, and so on. However, these methods do not fully leverage the power of corpora, i.e., large collections of text, which contain rich information about word usage and language patterns. By contrast, recent advances in data-driven NLP, such as neural network models, have shown to effectively exploit abundant linguistic information in corpora by learning representations and features directly from data. However, many neural network models primarily rely on limited local context information (e.g., previous and following words) for POS tagging, ignoring the potential impact of broader corpus-wide information. Inspired by the breakthroughs in deep learning for various NLP tasks, such as sentiment analysis, machine translation, and language modeling, we explore incorporating more representative, informative features from corpora that can improve POS tagging accuracy. Intuitively, various corpus-wide statistics could contain useful information for POS tagging. For instance, word embeddings, which capture semantic context and linguistic properties of words, can provide a dense continuous representation of each word's linguistic characteristics. Machine reading comprehension (MRC) has evolved significantly over the past few years. Initially, it was focused on answering simple questions from well-edited texts. However, the rise of user-generated content on the internet has led to a shift towards answering real-world questions from users out of web data. In the real-world setting, the context for a question is not just a single document, but rather full-body text from multiple relevant documents in the top search results. These questions can range from asking for a single, short, and factual answer to seeking reasons, procedures, and opinions. Despite these differences, most existing MRC systems use traditional question-answering mechanisms that are not designed to handle these complexities. In particular, previous systems have focused on addressing the issue of multiple possible answers for a single question by recognizing only one correct answer from a set of possible answers. However, in the real world, multiple answers could be equally valid for a single question. In addition, each answer may occur multiple times in the context, which further complicates the MRC task. The main contribution of this paper is to propose a multi-answer multi-task framework that addresses these challenges. Our framework consists of two key components: a novel multi-answer loss function and a minimum risk training method for handling multi-occurrence answers. In the first component, we use different loss functions for multiple reference answers, which allows us to capture the ambiguities and complexities of real-world questions. The second component, minimum risk training, is used to solve the multi-occurrence problem of a single answer by maximizing the expected reward under different threat models. In addition, we also propose a simple heuristic passage extraction strategy to handle overlong documents, which can improve the overall performance of the MRC system. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework on the DuReader dataset, which is a large-scale real-world MRC dataset. On this dataset, our model achieves a significant improvement in ROUGE-L score, from 44.18, the previous state-of-the-art, to 51.09. This implies that our multi-answer multi-task framework can effectively address the complexities of real-world MRC tasks and improve the overall performance of MRC systems. In the rest of this paper, we provide a detailed introduction to the background of MRC, followed by a description of our proposed framework and the experiments conducted to evaluate its performance. In Section 2, we provide a detailed background of MRC, including the motivations and challenges behind the real-world setting. In Section 3, we introduce our proposed multi-answer multi-task framework, including the multi-answer loss function and the minimum risk training method. In Section 4, we present our experiments on the DuReader dataset, including the model settings and evaluation results. In Section 5, we discuss the implications of our findings and provide directions for future research. Finally, in Section 6, we conclude the paper with a summary of the main contributions. Traditional approaches to JERE typically employ a two-stage pipeline: first, extract entities using named entity recognition (NER) models (Ratinov and Roth, 2009); then, use relation extraction models to identify relations between extracted entities (Zhou et al., 2005). However, this pipeline-based approach has several limitations: the accuracy of the first-stage entity recognition is often low, and the results from the first stage can also lead to inaccurate relation extraction in the second stage. Moreover, prior approaches have been found to lack a unified framework that can effectively capture the interactions between entities and relations. On the other hand, recent advances in deep learning have shown great successin many NLP tasks, including entity recognition and relation extraction (Turian et al., 2010;Socher et al., 2013). In particular, neural network models have achieved impressive results for tasks such as sentiment analysis (Hochreiter et al., 2001) and chunking (Collobert et al., 2011), demonstrating their potential for modeling complex linguistic phenomena. Given the impressive success of deep learning methods in related NLP tasks, it is natural to consider the integration of these approaches for JERE. However, straightforward application of deep learning models to JERE would require careful selection of model architectures and hyperparameters to ensure effective extraction of entities and relations. Recent investigations have proposed supervised modeling architectures that integre entity and relation extraction (Li and Ji, 2014). However, these models tend to be complex, hard to train and harder to be interpret the results of each prediction step. To address this issue, we investigate a new lightweight joint learning paradigm based on Minimum Risk Training (MRT). Specifically, our algorithm optimizes a global loss function which allows efficient integration of the predictions from the entity model and the relationmodel. We implement a simple neural network architecture, which learns to perform joint entity and relation extraction by executing MRT on the global loss function. Semantic parsing from denotations (SPD) represents a fundamental natural language understanding challenge. Specifically, given a natural language input (e.g., a question), the goal of SPD is to infer the related semantic parse that corresponds to a plausible extension of a formal knowledge base (KB). SPD has received significant attention in recent years due to its wide application potential in areas such as question-answering systems, conversational dialogue systems, and intelligentbots. The main challenge in SPD is to develop algorithms that can effectively learn to map natural language inputs to meaningful semantic parses. However, this task is extremely challenging due to the complexity and variety of natural language, the richness of semantics, and the sparsity of annotations. In recent years, various SPD algorithms have been proposed, which can be roughly categorized into two types: strategy-based methods (e.g., (Chen et al., 2018;Xu et al., 2019)) and model-based methods (e.g., (Li et al., 2018;Liang et al., 2018)). Although these methods have shown promising performance in SPD, they still suffer from at least two key limitations. Firstly, most SPD methods rely heavily on heavily engineered heavy machinery (x) used either in strategy-based methods find semantic parses that are likely to be correct only through exhaustive search in a predefined combinatorial space, which can be computationally infeasible for real-world applications, or only through computationally expensive approximation processes in model-based methods, which may lead to solutions with much degraded quality. This is because search-based method essentially perform exhaustive search in the vast space of possible parses and computationally expensive search can only be made by expensive heuristics. In addition, almost all proposed SPD methods in the literature rely solely on gradient-based optimizers for model training, which might get stuck in poor local optima particularly for complex compositional spaces of semantic parses. Moreover, model interpretability currently remains a major lacuna in SPD. To address the first challenge, we propose to leverage policy shaping (Haarnoja et al., 2018) to bias the search towards more plausible semantic parses that are compatible with the text. If they are, we reward the SPD model accordingly through policy shaping, otherwise we keep searching for more plausible parses. Semantic parsing is the task of mapping a sentence to a representation that allows for reasoning and inference about the meaning of the input sentence. In other words, semantic parsing aims to go beyond identifying the basic components (such as parts-of-speech) of a sentence and to build a representation that models the meaning relationships and underlying concepts of the sentence. This representation is often in the form of a semantic graph, which is a data structure consisting of nodes representing entities and relationships between these entities. There has been significant work on semantic parsing in various domains, using different approaches and techniques. However, most of these methods rely on the availability of manual data or annotated corpora, which can be time-consuming and expensive to create. Further, existing semantic parsing models are typically modular and sequential, which may not fully capture the complex interdependencies between entities and relationships in a sentence. Recently, there have been several promising directions for semantic parsing that aim to overcome these limitations. One such direction is the use of semantic graphs to represent the meaning of a sentence. Seman- tic graphs can capture the complex interdependencies between entities and relationships in a sentence, and can be tightly coupled with knowledge bases to take advantage of the vast relevant knowledge. On the other hand, another promising direction for semantic parsing is the use of neural network models to map sentences to semantic representations. These neural models can be trained end-to-end, leveraging the powerful representation learning and prediction ability of neural networks. In particular, Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) models have been shown to be effective for modeling long-range dependencies in sequences, which is essential for semantic parsing. In this paper, we propose a neural semantic parsing approach called Sequence-to-Action, which models semantic parsing as an end-to-end semantic graph generation process. Our method combines the advantages of both directions: we use a semantic graph to represent the meaning of a sentence, and we leverage the powerful representation learning and prediction ability of RNN models. Concretely, our method consists of two main components: (a) a sequence encoder to map sentences to a sequence of actions that are relevant for semantic graph generation, and (b) a graph builder to take these actions and generate a semantic graph. The sequence encoder is based on a bi-directional RNN, which can effectively capture the local and long-range dependencies in a sentence. The input to the RNN is a sequence of tokens from a sentence, which can be obtained from a language model. The output of the RNN is a sequence of actions, which are represented as tokens in a vocabulary. The graph builder takes the output sequence of actions and generates a semantic graph. The graph builder can be thought of as a parser, which interleaves the actions in the output sequence to build a graph. The graph builder starts with an empty graph and then iteratively applies the actions from the output sequence to the graph, ensuring that the graph is always valid (i.e., it does not contain any edges between unrelated entities). The key insight behind our method is that the RNN model can learn to generate a sequence of actions that are relevant for semantic graph generation. It usually employs a scoring function $ s_{\theta}(x, y) = f( x | \theta) $, which represents how well the predicted output $ y $ matches the actual output for a given input $ x $, parameterized by the model $ \theta $. Twitter, a microblogging platform with over 330 million active users worldwide (as of April 2023), has become a rich source of information on various events and trends, making it a valuable resource for text mining and topic modeling. The vast amount of user-generated content on Twitter presents both an opportunity and a challenge for topic modeling. On one hand, Twitter data provides a wide range of topics and themes that can be extracted and analyzed using various topic modeling techniques. On the other hand, the short length and ephemeral nature of tweets make it challenging to extract meaningful topics and themes. To address this challenge, researchers have proposed various topic modeling techniques, including the Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) model (Blei et al., 2003). LDA is a popular topic modeling technique that assumes that each document (in this case, a collection of tweets) consists of a mixture of topics, where each topic is a distribution over a set of words (Blei et al., 2003). However, when LDA is applied to Twitter data, it generally treats all aggregated tweets of a user as a single document. This can lead to poor topic modeling results, as it fails to capture the nuances of individual user interests and topic trends. To address this limitation, Twitter-LDA has been proposed (Sasaki et al., 2013). Twitter-LDA assumes that each tweet is a single topic and uses a single topic to represent a tweet. This approach has shown to be superior in topic semantic coherence (Sasaki et al., 2013). However, Twitter-LDA has a major limitation - it is not capable of online inference. Online inference is a critical requirement for topic modeling on Twitter, as it enables the model to adapt to changing user interests and topic trends in real-time. To address this limitation, we propose an online topic model for Twitter that incorporates the dynamics of user interests and topic trends. Our model extends Twitter-LDA in two ways. First, we model the generation process of tweets more accurately by estimating the ratio between topic words and general words for each user. This enables the model to capture the nuances of individual user interests and topic trends. Second, we use the topic tracking model (TTM) (Bradley and Bennett, 2004) to enable online inference. TTM is a probabilistic graphical model that models consumer purchase behaviors, which we adapt to model user interests and topic trends on Twitter. Our proposed model, which we term Online-Twitter-LDA, uses a hierarchical Bayesian framework to capture the dynamics of user interests and topic trends. The model consists of two levels - the user level and the topic level. At the user level, we use a stick-breaking process to model the distribution of topics for each user. At the topic level, we use the Dirichlet process to model the distribution of words for each topic. This enables the model to capture the nuances of individual user interests and topic trends. The contribution of this paper is two-fold. Firstly, we propose an online topic model for Twitter that captures the dynamics of user interests and topic trends. Secondly, we show that our proposed model outperforms existing topic modeling techniques in terms of topic semantic coherence and online inference ability. The experimental results demonstrated that our model is capable of adapt to changing user interests and topic trends in real-time, making it a valuable tool for a wide range of applications, including user profiling, event summarization, and topic tracking.

Enabling a computer to understand a document so that it can answer comprehension questions is a central, yet unsolved goal of Natural Language Processing (NLP). Reading comprehension, in particular, has been a long-standing challenge in NLP, as it requires a deep understanding of the passage and the ability to directly answer questions based on the information presented in the passage. Despite significant advances in recent years, reading comprehension remains an open problem in NLP. Traditional reading comprehension datasets, such as the MCTest dataset (Richardson et al., 2013), contain only a few hundred training examples, which is insufficient for training large neural networks. To address this issue, Hermann et al. (2015) proposed a novel approach to creating a large-scale reading comprehension dataset. Specifically, they paired news articles from the CNN and Daily Mail with their summarized bullet points to create a large corpus of text passages with question-answer pairs. This corpus, known as the CNN/Daily Mail dataset, contains over a million training examples, making it one of the largest reading comprehension datasets to date. Hermann et al. demonstrated that a neural network can be trained on this dataset to achieve good performance on the reading comprehension task. Our analysis reveals that the task requires not only understanding of the passage, but also reasoning and inference abilities. Second, we develop and evaluate simple, carefully designed systems for reading comprehension. Our goal is to push the boundaries of what is currently possible on this task and to provide a baseline for future research. Traditional methods for entity linking relied heavily on hand-engineered features, such as lexical features, context features, and entity types, which were often domain-specific and required significant manual effort to construct. Recent advancements in neural machine translation (NMT) have led to stateof-the-art performance in various benchmarks. A key challenge in NMT is effectively utilizing contextual information to improve translation quality. In this paper, we propose a hierarchical attention model to capture document-level contextual information in a structured and dynamic manner, and integrate it into the original NMT architecture as another level of abstraction. Our hierarchical attention model conditions on the NMT model's own previous hidden states, allowing for a sequential and incremental learning process. This contrasts with traditional attention models, which learn a single, static alignment across the entire document. By applying the hierarchical attention model at multiple levels of abstraction, we can effectively learn to model the intricate structure of context in a document. Our model can capture the prominence of specific words or phrases in a document, recognizing which parts of the context are most relevant for a given sentence during decoding. This enables the model to focus on and build upon the contextually most informative material in the previous sentences and paragraphs. Our model, which we call Document-Level NMT with Hierarchical Attention (DL-NMT-HA), consists of two key components: a word-level NMT model that learns to translate individual sentences, and a hierarchical attention module that captures context at the phrase or sentence level. Specifically, the hierarchical attention module consists of two sub-modules: a higher-level attention module that assigns importance weights to different phrases or sentences in the source document based on their relevance to the current sentence, and a lower-levelattention module that selects the most relevant word from each assigned phrase or sentence. We integrate the hierarchical attention module into the original NMT architecture, using the output of the higher-level attention module to condition the decoder's weights and bias on the context that is most relevant for a given sentence. This allows the decoder to learn to incorporate context in a structured and dynamic manner, taking into account both the sequential and compositional nature of context. We conduct experiments on a large-scale machine translation dataset, comparing the performance ofDL-NMT-HA to a strong NMT baseline, as well as to other context-aware methods that use pre-computed context embeddings. We also conduct an ablation study to demonstrate that both the encoder and decoder benefit from the context captured by the hierarchical attention module in complementary ways. Our findings indicate that the use of hierarchical attention in NMT can lead to significant improvements in translation quality, and that this improvement is both robust and complementary across different levels of abstraction and model components. Sentence compression is a natural language processing (NLP) task that allows for the automatic summarization of text. A compressor system takes an input sentence and produces a shorter and simplified version while maintaining the same meaning as the original sentence. Traditional sentence compression is typically carried out in a monolingual setting where the goal is to simplify a sentence from a single language. However, with the advent of the globalized digital era, multilingual natural language processing (NLP) tasks have become increasingly important (Napoles et al., 2017). In many real-world applications, such as machine translation and multilingual information retrieval, it would be beneficial to take advantage of bilingual information to improve the efficiency of sentence compression. In this paper, we explore the problem of sentence compression in a bilingual setting and propose two methods to handle parallel sentences (i.e., two sentences in the same language but with different meanings or translations). Our main hypothesis is that bilingual sentence compression can be an asset for a variety of multilingual NLP tasks, namely: more accurate machine translation by providing higher quality outputs and improved paraphrasing and question answering systems, through the provision of a more precise semantics. Another major goal of this work is to experimentally assess the benefits of bilingual sentence compression based on efficiency, which would be to demonstrate whether certain bilingual compressed sentences represent better simplifications of sentences as understood by humans. Since compressions of the parallel sentences should preserve the original meaning of both expressions, bilingual sentence compression is also a new tool to alleviate what is often referred to as the lack of parallel data. We propose two bilingual extension methods to the classical monolingual compressor. The goal of this work is to: a) introduce the bilingual sentence compression problem, b) explain how the proposed bilingual extension methods operate, and c) present a real-world application of these methods in a parallel corpus of news articles. On a practical level, the most direct contribution of our work is the development of bilingual sentence compression systems. On the theoretical level, the most interesting contribution of this work to the field, is to provide the first compelling runs for assessing the effects of sentence fusion and sentence splitting on the qualities of bilingual compression systems. Sentence compression operates by removing redundant phrases or redundant words often referred to as stop words from the initial sentence to produce a shorter target sentence that contains more meaning and this meaning is the same as the meaning contained by the initial sentence. Stop words make up a significant portion of any sentence but contribute minimally to its meaning. For example, given the sentence "The sun, which is shining brightly in the sky, sets on the Tokyo bay," a possible compressed sentence would be "The sun shines brightly in the sky and sets on Tokyo bay." Feature representation is a critical component in statistical machine translation (SMT), as it directly influences the performance of the translation model. Generally, features are designed manually based on linguistic knowledge, domain experience, and intuition, and can include a variety of hand-crafted representations, such as phrase translations, tags, and part-of-speech (POS) labels. These features can be manually calculated and are then used to train the SMT model. However, these hand-crafted representations can be time-consuming and costly to develop, and may not effectively capture the complex relationships between different parts of a sentence. Recent advances in deep learning have shown that data-driven representations learned by the model can be more effective and robust than hand-crafted features (Bengio et al., 2003). In particular, the deep autoencoder (DAE) paradigm (Hinton and Salakhutdinov, 2009) has been widely used for unsupervised feature learning. In this paradigm, a deep neural network is trained to reconstruct the input data from a lower-dimensional representation, and in the process, the network learns to capture relevant information about the input data. The learned features can then be used as input to the SMT model. Deep belief nets (DBNs) (Hinton et al., 2006) are a type of feedforward neural network that can be used as a pre-training step for the DAE. DBNs consist of multiple layers of restricted Boltzmann machines (RBMs), and the weights of the RBM layers are learned in a hierarchical manner by maximizing the likelihood of the input data. The resulting DBN can be fine-tuned on the labeled data to adjust the weights to match the target supervised task. In this paper, we present a semi-supervised learning approach that learns new features using a DAE paradigm for phrase-based translation models. Our system first pre-trains the deep autoencoder (DAE) parameters using an unsupervised deep belief net (DBN), and then fine-tunes the DAE using the input original phrase features as a teacher for semi-supervised learning. This allows the model to learn the structure of the input data, and the relationships between different parts of a sentence. We also introduce a novel feature composition approach to learn high-dimensional features by combining multiple DAEs. Our approach is data-driven, and the features are learned from the training data without requiring any manual design or engineering effort. Our experiments on two Chinese-English tasks show that our semi-supervised DAE features obtain significant improvements over the unsupervised DBN features and the baseline features, respectively. This demonstrates the effectiveness of our approach in learning more effective and stable features for SMT. There are many benefits to using learning based feature representation for SMT, including requiring less manual design effort, providing the ability to model complex relationships between different parts of a sentence, and helping discover new knowledge about translation tasks. Our results provide evidence that learning based feature representation can be quite effective in improving SMT performance. Another advantage of using learning based features is that they do not require fixed feature definition (Xia, 2006), which are inherently limited to only learnable function types e.g., functions mapping one continuous vector to another continuous vector.assistant In addition, while our current implementation uses the existing phrase-based SMT framework, DAE features have the potential to be directly integrated with other frameworks, such as neural network-based approaches, to further improve translation

However, these models do not inherently guarantee the generation of diverse or informative responses, which remains a significant challenge. Unlike traditional GAN-based models, our approach incorporates the sequence-to-sequence framework to train a response generative model that modifies existing responses into novel ones. Sequential labeling is a challenging task in natural language processing (NLP), as it requires both capturing the contextual dependencies between input tokens and simultaneously predicting a sequence of outputs. Applications of sequential labeling include part-of-speech tagging, named entity recognition, and machine translation, to name a few. While deep learning models have achieved remarkable success in these areas, they often rely on large amounts of labeled data, which can be expensive and time-consuming to obtain. Semi-supervised learning approaches can potentially overcome this limitation by leveraging unlabeled data to improve model performance. Recent years have seen a surge of interest in semi-supervised learning methods for sequential labeling. Many of these methods exploit the idea that the same model can be used to generate self-supervisory signals from unlabeled data, which are then used to train the model. However, an important caveat of this approach is that it may not fully capture the inherent structure of the sequential data, and can be limited by the lack of nuanced label-specific information. These challenges motivate the need for models that can more effectively leverage both supervised and unsupervised signals to improve sequential labeling performance. In this paper, we introduce a family of variational methods for semi-supervised sequence labeling that incorporates both a generative and a discriminative component. The generative component is responsible for modeling the conditional probability of a word given its context, drawing inspiration from word prediction objectives commonly used in learning word embeddings. The discriminative component is a learned function that helps inject label-specific information into the latent space. Our models can be viewed as multitask variants of the variational autoencoder (VAE), where the inference and generative processes are shared across multiple outputs. We explore different latent variable configurations, including ones with hierarchical structure that enables the model to capture both label-specific and word-specific information. Our experimental results show that our models consistently outperform standard sequential baselines on 8 sequence labeling datasets, and improve further with unlabeled data. In particular, we find that our models are particularly effective at incorporating latent structure, even in cases where the discriminative component is not explicitly given access to this structure. This suggests that our models are well-suited to a wide range of sequential labeling tasks, and can provide a valuable tool for NLP practitioners seeking to leverage unlabeled data to improve model performance. We also experiment with combining our models with other types of semi-supervised learning methods, and find that this can lead to even further improvements in performance. Overall, our results suggest that our variational sequential labelers are a powerful tool for semi-supervised sequence labeling, and we look forward to exploring their potential further in future work. Sentiment analysis, a fundamental NLP task, seeks to determine the emotional tone or attitude conveyed by a text. Recent endeavors have shifted focus from traditional aspect-based sentiment analysis (Lim et al., 2005) to document-level sentiment analysis (Kim, 2014), where the goal is to assign a sentiment polarity score to the entire document, taking into account all relevant passages. This paradigm addresses the issue that sentiment can vary across different parts of a document, meaning a single sentence can exhibit multiple emotions such as gratitude and negativity. Capturing these nuanced aspects of sentiment is essential for high-quality sentiment analysis. Specifically, the latent subjectivity modeling approach, which aims to model the underlying subjective emotional content without annotations, has gained significant traction (Precup and Sutton, 2009;Schmitt and Schraft, 2013;Herskovic et al., 2013). This paradigm learns latent subjectivity variables and associates word features or co-occurrence patterns with sentiment shifts. Despite the promising results, however, latent variable models fail to harness our existing in-depth understanding of discourse structure and linguistic knowledge (e.g., Halliday and Hasan, 1978). It is crucial to notice that, in a discourse, various discourse connectors like "but", "however", "in addition", and "meanwhile" often serve as crucial sentences to modify the subjectivity of a text. These elements may signal attitude shifts or changes in focus that impact the final sentiment polarity score. A remarkable challenge in this area is learning a robust representation for event patterns that generalize across different domains, entities, and timescales. Most existing methods for learning event representations rely on a large amount of human-annotated event data. While group-level tasks such as event classification can be addressed through weak supervision, tasks that require predicting precise event structures or relationships remain challenging. One of the most significant challenges is that there is a lack of annotated data that not only includes event details but also the relationships among events. Moreover, even data that does include annotations of the relationships between events may lack the intricate relational information needed to model complex event structures. Existing representations for events, such as entity-relation graphs and event jets, fail to capture these complex relationships (Johnson et al., 2008;Ash et al., 2011). Another challenge that makes it hard to learn a robust event representation is the occurrence of rare event patterns. Unlike frequent patterns, which are often in short periodic cycles, rare event patterns exhibit non-periodic patterns, leading to the great difficulty to predict when and where they occur (Kumar, 2004). Considering these challenges, learning a distributed representation for event patterns is essential and has some important applications, such as: (1) preprocessing event discovery: a robust event representation can automatically generate patterns for event discovery: (2) text generation: with such representations, event-based text generation is easier than ever;(3) decision-making systems: by learning a robust event representation, the accuracy and robustness of decision-making systems significantly improve. Dependency parsing is a prominent task in natural language processing (NLP), with a wide range of applications in text analysis, information extraction, and machine translation. Despite significant advances in recent years, parsing is still a challenging problem, especially for certain types of languages or syntactic structures. A key factor contributing to the difficulty of this task is the diversity of dependencies in a given sentence. Some dependencies are relatively easy to predict, while others require more complex analysis and deeper understanding of linguistic structures. The analysis of scientific rhetoric has been a long-standing problem in the natural language processing (NLP) community. Recent advances in deep learning and neural networks have opened up new opportunities for automated analysis of rhetorical structures in text. Scientific writing, in particular, is a unique genre that blends formal language with persuasive elements, making it an attractive target for rhetorical analysis (Charney and Pizzato, 2000). Recent work on scientific text analysis has focused on segmenting text into potential rhetorical moves, identifying literary devices such as allusions and hyperbole, and even discovering the relationships between authors and reviewers (Das and Smith, 2009;Yang et al., 2016). However, these approaches have largely focused on isolating specific features or components of scientific rhetoric, without exploring their interplay and complex relationships. Argumentation, a critical component of scientific writing, is particularly difficult to model due to the subtlety and nuance of its often implicit and contextualized expressions (Linde, 2001;Snoeck et al., 2009). Moreover, in contrast to formal argumentation theory, scientific argumentation often reveals itself through the performative and material aspects of scientific discourse (Perakis and Aloimonos, 2013). In this paper, we set out to investigate the relationship between the argumentative structure of scientific publications and various rhetorical aspects, including discourse categories and citation contexts. To this end, we will introduce two new components to the analysis: (1) an augmented corpus of scientific publications annotated with four layers of rhetoric annotations, and (2) a neural multi-task learning architecture that combines argument extraction with a set of rhetorical classification tasks. Our hypothesis is that a multi-task learning framework can capture the interplay between argumentation and rhetorical features, ultimately leading to improved performance across a range of tasks related to scientific rhetoric analysis. We further assume that by coupling the extraction of argumentative components with various rhetorical classification tasks, a joint model can learn to leverage the relationships between these components and improve the generality of its predictions. The specific contributions of this paper can be summarized as follows. The domain of opinion detection has been a thriving area of research in natural language processing (NLP), with advances in recent years that have greatly improved the performance of various systems in extracting opinions from text. However, despite these advancements, there remains a crucial component of opinion that remains largely unexplored: the perspective of the user of an opinion-mining system as to what an opinion truly is. This component, which we refer to as metasubjectivity, is a multifaceted issue that goes to the heart of the very notion of opinion itself. Machine translation (MT) evaluation is a crucial task in the field of natural language processing. MT evaluation metrics are used to estimate the quality of a machine translation system by comparing the produced translation with a human reference translation. Among these metrics, METEOR (Banerjee and Lavie, 2005) is particularly popular due to its ability to consider synonymy and morphological similarity between the automatic and reference translations. However, METEOR has limitations in understanding the potential subtleties in language. To overcome these limitations and provide a more comprehensive evaluation, researchers have proposed integrating external lexico-semantic resources into MT evaluation metrics. One such approach is the use of lexical resources like WordNet (Fellbaum, 1998) and DBnary (Navigli, 2009). By incorporating these resources, evaluation metrics can identify meanings that may not be explicitly mentioned but can be inferred through the use of lexical and semantic relationships. Nevertheless, these resources require significant storage and updating efforts to stay current. Recent advances in word representation techniques have provided an alternative for augmenting MT evaluation metrics. Pre-trained vector representations, such as Word2Vec (Mikolov et al., 2013) and GloVe (Pennington et al., 2014), have been shown to capture certain nuances in language. These vectors have been found to be effective in capturing similar semantic relationships as lexical resources. However, the real challenge is deciding which type of augmenting method to use: incorporating lexico-semantic resources or distributed representations of words. In this paper, we investigate the impact of both approaches on the performance of METEOR in evaluating machine translations. Our experiments are conducted in the context of the Metrics task of the Workshop on Machine Translation (WMT) 2014. We consider the metrics tasks of translating news stories from German and Czech into English. We compare the results of the augmented METEOR versions using vector representations and DBnary. The results of our experiments show that the distributed representations are a good alternative to lexical resources, bringing interesting additional information to the METEOR evaluation metric. Specifically, the effectiveness of vector representations in revealing more subtle semantic relationships becomes more apparent in longer sentences, pointing out the usefulness of static lexical representations as an alternative. Emotions are a natural and essential aspect of human experience, a vital element of emotional intelligence, and a cornerstone of human relationships. Emotion recognition in text is crucial for natural language processing applications such as sentiment analysis, affective computing, and opinion mining. While sentiment is a global evaluation of a text (negative or positive), emotions are more nuanced groupings within that global sentiment and can involve subtle and context-dependent feelings or intuitions (Moore and Piringer, 2007). Emotion classification from text relies heavily on word-emotion association, but existing emotion lexicons incur several disadvantages. Firstly, they are generally limited in their coverage of emotions and the words they pair with these emotional categories (Mohammad, 2018). This paucity of depth and breadth may therefore lead to shallow insights and a narrow perspective on emotions. Secondly, current methods for computing word-emotion association typically rely on pre-existing measures of semantic similarity (Koehler and Grah, 2008;Marshman et al., 2013) or hypothetical word pairs (Bora and Ag, 2012;Lucia, 2015). However, words can take on highly variable emotional meanings depending on their context and the population they are expressed in (Crane, 2013). Word representation is a critical component in many Natural Language Processing (NLP) tasks. Vector space models, which represent words as vectors in a high-dimensional space, have been widely used to capture the semantic relatedness of words. However, different forms of word relatedness, such as synonyms, antonyms, and hyponyms, are often represented in different vector spaces. This can result in the need to use multiple vector spaces and to manually curate the data needed for a particular application. In this work, we propose a novel method for synthesizing a single vector representation for each word that can be used to represent the concept of a word in a unified manner. Traditional word representation learning models, such as Word2Vec (Mikolov et al., 2013) and GloVe (Pennington et al., 2014), use fixed dimensionality and learn a single representation for each word that is shared across all word relatedness perspectives. However, it is well-known that words can have multiple, incompatible representations depending on the specific perspective, such as in cases where a word has both a more positive and a more negative connotation . In other words, when we observe a relevant pair of words, a heavy heart accompanies a depressed mood, while a heavy heart would not necessarily be seen as related to a depressed mood in a different perspective as for example, a cold day accompanying a depression despair is not seen as light hearted mood. In addition, as pointed by (Yin et al., 2009), these representations lack the expressiveness of models based on neural networks, which are able to capture even more complex relationships in data. The BPTF framework leverages low-rank tensor factorization to model the interaction between a set of word similarity matrices. Each matrix represents a specific perspective on word similarity, such as synonyms, antonyms, or co-occurrence. The BPTF framework learns a set of latent factors that capture the relationships between words across different perspectives, and a set of per-perspective linear transformations that transform the latent factors into word vectors in each vector space.
