Language modeling is a fundamental task in natural language processing (NLP), with applications in summarization, machine translation, dialogue systems, and other areas. The goal of language modeling is to assign a probability distribution over sequences of words in a language, which can then be used in conjunction with other NLP models to perform tasks like language generation, sentiment analysis, and part-of-speech tagging [Kneser and Ney, 1995]. Historically, language modeling has been performed using count-based n-gram models, where the probability of a word is calculated based on its n-1 preceding words [Jelinek and Mercer, 1980, Manning and Schutze, 1999]. These models have several advantages, including their ability to score word sequences extremely quickly and their suitability for large-vocabulary languages. However, these models also have significant limitations. They suffer from the curse of dimensionality, and the number of parameters often explodes as the size of the vocabulary increases [Cestnik, 1990]. Moreover, traditional n-gram models ignore the sequential dependencies between symbols, which is a major drawback, since words often exhibit complex patterns and relationships that cannot be captured using simple n-gram counts. On the other hand, neural language models have become increasingly popular in recent years, and have demonstrated significant improvements over traditional n-gram models in many applications. Neural language models use a neural network to learn the probability distribution of words based on their contextual relationships with surrounding words, leading to more accurate and nuanced modeling [Bengio et al., 2003, Mikolov et al., 2010]. However, these models also have significant limitations. They often require large amounts of training data, which can be expensive to obtain, and are computationally expensive to train and evaluate [Jozefowicz et al., 2016]. They also suffer from low interpretability and the challenge of learning representations that generalize well to unseen scenarios. Recently, researchers have begun exploring the use of hybrid models that combine the strengths of traditional n-gram models and neural language models. For example, some researchers have proposed models that use a shallow neural network to adapt the weights of an n-gram model based on the input word sequence [Li et al., 2014]. Another approach is to use a more complex neural network to predict the probability distribution over n-grams [Kim et al., 2015]. However, these approaches often require significant additions to the neural architecture and can result in model complexity. This paper proposes a new approach to hybridizing count-based n-gram models and neural language models. We propose a framework in which both types of models are combined using a mixture distribution, allowing us to define a set of probability distributions over the vocabulary of words and then dynamically calculate mixture weights over these distributions. Our approach is different from previous methods in that it provides a general framework for combining the strengths of traditional n-gram models and neural language models, without requiring significant additions to the neural architecture. In this paper, we describe the formulation of our hybrid model, referred to as a mixture language model. We then present experimental results demonstrating the effectiveness of our model, as well as comparisons with traditional n-gram models and neural language models. Multi-document summarization is a challenging task that involves extracting the most informative and relevant content from a large collection of documents. Traditional summarization techniques focus on individual documents, and may fail to capture the relationships and dependencies between different documents in a category. A key insight in this paper is that documents belonging to the same category often share common information, such as lexical patterns, thematic concepts and relationships, that are not present in documents from other categories. This category-specific information can be a useful cue for identifying sentences that are relevant and important for summarization. Recent studies (Das et al., 2007;Cafarella et al., 2008) have applied the concept of category-specific importance (CSI) to multi-document summarization tasks. However, CSI is typically computed manually, requiring human judgment and extensive domain knowledge, which limits its applicability to general summarization tasks. These features capture the degree to which a sentence is similar to other sentences in the same category, and the extent to which it aligns with the dominant topics and themes in that category, respectively. By incorporating these features into the sentence selection process, we can effectively encode the category-specific information without any need for manual annotation or inference. Discourse relations are a fundamental concept in Natural Language Processing (NLP), representing the relationships between different segments of text that convey ideas, arguments, or points of view. Identifying discourse relations is crucial for various text-level NLP applications, such as text summarization, question answering, and information extraction (cf. Hovy and Gaizauskas (2001)). Discourse relations are often categorized into two types: explicit and implicit (Asher and Lascarides, 2003). Explicit discourse relations are those where a connective or rhetorical marker, such as "because", "however" or "in addition to", explicitly states the relationship between the two segments. Implicit discourse relations, on the other hand, are those where the relationship between the segments is not explicitly marked. Identifying implicit discourse relations is a challenging task, as they often require contextual information and world knowledge to be understood correctly (cf. Lin et al., 2010). In this work, we present a variant of a neural model, which we call Variational Neural Discourse Relation Recognizer, to automatically identify both explicit and implicit discourse relations in text. Unlike traditional approaches that rely heavily on feature engineering and manual annotation (cf. Bunescu et al., 2005), our model is a type of deep learning model that can automatically learn the underlying patterns in language from large amounts of text data. Concretely, we propose a hybrid model that combines a pointer sentinel mechanism (Andor et al., 2016) and a markov random field (Murphy, 2002). To model the conditional probability over the discourse relations, we utilize a conditional random field (Lafferty et al., 2001) supervised by annotated discourse relations from the Penn Discourse Treebank (Prasad et al., 2008). The vanilla version of our model shows state-of-the-art performance on the Penn Discourse Treebank. Moreover, our results support that the proposed architecture is more proficient in identifying implicit discourse relations than recognizing explicit discourse relations.
